\chapter{The First Verbs}
\label{ch:first-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{5}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can conjugate any regular German verb, ask where someone lives and what they are doing, and build my own present-tense sentences instead of reciting them.}

Until now the book handed over fixed phrases. This chapter hands over the machine: take the -en off a German verb and the stem that is left accepts six endings, learned once and applied to thousands of words. Three verbs run through it — wohnen, machen, lernen — along with the pronouns the paradigm needs and the question words wo and was. It ends with Ich lerne Deutsch, the first sentence in the book assembled from parts nobody handed over whole, and with the reason German keeps its pronoun when Spanish drops it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[wohnen]{wohnen — \textquotedblleft{}to live,\textquotedblright{} and your first regular verb}

\label{lesson:GE-C05-wohnen}



\begin{quote}
Until now you have assembled fixed phrases. This chapter hands you the machine itself — and the first verb to run through it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: wohnen}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{wohnen} — \textquotedblleft{}to live, to dwell.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Not \emph{to be alive} — that is a different verb. \emph{Wohnen} is where your bed is.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{w-as-v} — the \textbf{w} is an English \emph{v}.
  \item \texttt{h-silent-lengthening} — the \textbf{h} only stretches the \emph{o}, exactly as in \emph{gehen} and \emph{sehen}.
\end{itemize}

So: \emph{VOH-nen}, with a long open \emph{oh}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{wohnen} comes from Old High German \emph{wonēn}, \textquotedblleft{}to dwell, to be accustomed, to be content\textquotedblright{} — because dwelling somewhere and \emph{being used to} it were the same idea.

That root survives in English, just barely, in \textbf{wont}: \textquotedblleft{}as is his \emph{wont}\textquotedblright{} means \textquotedblleft{}as he is accustomed.\textquotedblright{} It is also kin to \textbf{win} and \textbf{wish} — all from one root about striving for something, or being content with it.

So \emph{wohnen} is not a stranger. It is the word behind \emph{wont}, still doing the older job.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}wohnen\textquotedblright{} (\emph{VOH-nen}) — \emph{v}, then a long \emph{oh}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}wohnen\textquotedblright{} and English \textquotedblleft{}wont\textquotedblright{} — accustomed, at home
  \item \textquotedblleft{}wohnen\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}gehen\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}sehen\textquotedblright{} — three verbs, one silent \emph{h}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{wohnen} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To live, to dwell.\textquotedblright{}) Which English word is it? (\emph{Wont} — accustomed.) What does the \emph{h} do? (Only lengthens the \emph{o}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der Stamm]{der Stamm — drop the \emph{-en}, and you have the machine}

\label{lesson:GE-C05-verbstamm}



\begin{quote}
You met the ending-swap on \emph{heißen}. Here is the piece underneath it, and it is the reason the swap works on every verb.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the stem}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{The stem} is what is left when you take \textbf{-en} off the dictionary form.
\end{quote}

\emph{wohnen} minus \emph{-en} leaves \textbf{wohn-}. That is the part that never changes. The endings attach to it, and the dictionary form you look up is simply the stem already wearing one of them.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the three singular endings}]
Take \emph{wohn-} and add:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Person} & \textbf{Ending} & \textbf{Form} \\
\midrule
\emph{ich} & \textbf{-e} & \emph{ich wohne} \\
\emph{du} & \textbf{-st} & \emph{du wohnst} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You saw \emph{-e} on \emph{ich heiße}. The \emph{-st} was hiding: \emph{heißen} ends in \textbf{ß}, and \emph{ß + st} collapses to \emph{heißt}, so \emph{du heißt} never showed you the \emph{s}. On a normal stem it is plain — \emph{du wohnst}.

This is not special to \emph{wohnen}. Every regular verb in German runs exactly this, which is why learning one is learning thousands. Grammars call these \textbf{weak} verbs — \textquotedblleft{}weak\textquotedblright{} because they take their endings meekly instead of changing their vowel the way \emph{strong} verbs do. You will meet a strong one soon enough.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}wohnen\textquotedblright{} then the stem — \textquotedblleft{}wohn-\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich wohne\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}du wohnst\textquotedblright{}
  \item the endings alone — \emph{-e}, \emph{-st}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you get the stem? (Drop \emph{-en}.) What is the stem of \emph{wohnen}? (\emph{Wohn-}.) Which endings go with \emph{ich} and \emph{du}? (\emph{-e} and \emph{-st}.) Why did \emph{du heißt} not show the \emph{s}? (\emph{ß} and \emph{st} collapse together.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[er · sie · es]{er · sie · es — \textquotedblleft{}he,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}she,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}it,\textquotedblright{} and one ending for all three}

\label{lesson:GE-C05-er-sie-es}



\begin{quote}
You can talk about yourself and to one other person. To talk \emph{about} someone you need three more pronouns — and you already own one of them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: er, sie, es}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{er} — \textquotedblleft{}he.\textquotedblright{} Said \emph{air}, with the soft German \emph{r}.
\end{quote}

It pairs with the article you already know: \textbf{der} things are \emph{er} things.

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{sie} — \textquotedblleft{}she.\textquotedblright{} Said \emph{zee}.
\end{quote}

Yes: the same sound and spelling as the polite \emph{Sie}, and as the \emph{sie} meaning \textquotedblleft{}they.\textquotedblright{} German really does run three jobs through one word, and only the capital and the verb ending tell them apart. You will meet that properly later; for now, small \textbf{sie} with a \emph{-t} ending means \textbf{she}.

The three pronouns line up with the three articles, which is the whole reason German bothers with genders:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Article} & \textbf{Pronoun} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{der} & \emph{er} & he \\
\emph{die} & \emph{sie} & she \\
\emph{das} & \emph{es} & it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: all three take -t}]
One ending covers all three — attach \textbf{-t} to the stem:

\begin{quote}
\emph{er wohnt} · \emph{sie wohnt} · \emph{es wohnt}
\end{quote}

English does the same thing with \emph{-s} (\emph{he lives}, \emph{she lives}, \emph{it lives}) and nowhere else in the paradigm. German's \emph{-t} is that same odd little marker.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}er\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}sie\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}es\textquotedblright{} — he, she, it
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der/er\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}die/sie\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}das/es\textquotedblright{} — article, then pronoun
  \item \textquotedblleft{}er wohnt\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}sie wohnt\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}es wohnt\textquotedblright{} — one ending, three people
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which pronoun goes with \emph{der}? (\emph{Er}.) With \emph{die}? (\emph{Sie}.) What ending do all three take? (\emph{-t} — \emph{er wohnt}.) Which English ending does the same job? (\emph{-s}, as in \emph{he lives}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[wir]{wir — \textquotedblleft{}we,\textquotedblright{} and an ending you have already been saying}

\label{lesson:GE-C05-wir}



\begin{quote}
Three singular people down. Now the plural — and the first one is nearly free.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: wir}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{wir} — \textquotedblleft{}we.\textquotedblright{} Said \emph{veer}, with the \textbf{w} as a \emph{v} and the soft trailing \emph{r}, so it rhymes with \emph{mir} and \emph{dir}.
\end{quote}

It is English \textbf{we}, wearing German pronunciation. Nothing else to learn.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: wir takes -en}]
Attach \textbf{-en} to the stem:

\begin{quote}
\emph{wir wohnen}
\end{quote}

Which is the dictionary form, unchanged. German's infinitive and its \emph{wir} form are identical, for every regular verb — so half of this ending was already in your head before you met it.

You have seen this once: \emph{Sie heißen}, the polite form, is the same \emph{-en}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}wir\textquotedblright{} (\emph{veer}) — it rhymes with \textquotedblleft{}mir\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}dir\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}wohnen\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}wir wohnen\textquotedblright{} — the same word twice
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich wohne\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}du wohnst\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}er wohnt\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}wir wohnen\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{wir} mean, and what does it rhyme with? (\textquotedblleft{}We\textquotedblright{}; \emph{mir} and \emph{dir}.) Which ending does it take? (\emph{-en}.) What else looks exactly like \emph{wir wohnen}? (The dictionary form, \emph{wohnen}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ihr]{ihr — \textquotedblleft{}you all,\textquotedblright{} the plural English threw away}

\label{lesson:GE-C05-ihr}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Du} is one friend. What if there are several? English has no clean answer any more. German does.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ihr}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{ihr} — \textquotedblleft{}you all,\textquotedblright{} the plural of \emph{du}.
\end{quote}

Said \emph{eer}: the \textbf{h} is silent and lengthens the \emph{i}, the same trick as in \emph{Ihnen}.

Use it for a group you would each call \emph{du} — friends, family, a team. For a group of strangers you still use \emph{Sie}.

\begin{cousinweb}
English used to have this exact system and lost half of it. \emph{Thou} was the singular and \emph{ye}/\emph{you} the plural — then \emph{thou} faded, \emph{you} took over both jobs, and English was left unable to say \textquotedblleft{}you all\textquotedblright{} without inventing something: \emph{y'all}, \emph{you guys}, \emph{yous}, \emph{you lot}.

German never lost the distinction, so it needs no invention:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{Informal} & \textbf{Formal} \\
\midrule
one person & \emph{du} & \emph{Sie} \\
several people & \emph{ihr} & \emph{Sie} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: ihr takes -t}]
Attach \textbf{-t} to the stem:

\begin{quote}
\emph{ihr wohnt}
\end{quote}

The same \emph{-t} as \emph{er wohnt}. Two different people, one ending — so context, not the verb, tells you which is meant. That is the only place the German present tense is ever ambiguous, and the pronoun clears it up instantly.

The paradigm is now complete: \textbf{-e · -st · -t · -en · -t · -en}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ihr\textquotedblright{} (\emph{eer}) — you all
  \item \textquotedblleft{}du wohnst\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}ihr wohnt\textquotedblright{} — one friend, then several
  \item the whole six — wohne, wohnst, wohnt, wohnen, wohnt, wohnen
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{ihr} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}You all.\textquotedblright{}) Which English word did the same job before it was lost? (\emph{Ye} — leaving \emph{y'all} to fill the gap.) Which ending does \emph{ihr} share, and with whom? (\emph{-t}, with \emph{er/sie/es}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(the audible endings)]{The endings you can actually hear}

\label{lesson:GE-C05-endungen-hoerbar}



\begin{quote}
You have all six endings. Before moving on, one fact about them that makes German easier than it looks.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: German endings are audible}]
Say them aloud and they genuinely differ:

\begin{quote}
\emph{wohne} · \emph{wohnst} · \emph{wohnt} · \emph{wohnen}
\end{quote}

French writes just as many endings and pronounces almost none of them — \emph{parle}, \emph{parles}, \emph{parlent} are three spellings of one sound. A French listener gets the person from the pronoun alone, because the verb tells them nothing.

German is the opposite. The verb carries real information, and you could very nearly tell who is speaking from the ending by itself.

That is worth knowing for two reasons. It makes listening easier than reading at first, and it makes the \emph{next} question interesting: if German endings say who the subject is, why does German still insist on the pronoun? That is the end of this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}wohne\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}wohnst\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}wohnt\textquotedblright{} — three different sounds
  \item them again with your eyes closed, and hear the person change
  \item the full six in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Are German verb endings audible? (Yes — \emph{wohne}, \emph{wohnst}, \emph{wohnt} all differ.) And French ones? (Largely silent.) What does that let a German listener do? (Hear the person from the verb, not only the pronoun.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[in]{in — the word that did not change}

\label{lesson:GE-C05-in}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Ich wohne} — I live. Live \emph{where}? One more word and you have said something true about yourself.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: in}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{in} — \textquotedblleft{}in.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Same spelling, same meaning, near enough the same sound: a short \emph{i} as in English \emph{bit}. This is one of the small handful of words German and English never bothered to change.

You have already met its neighbour \emph{auf} (\textquotedblleft{}on\textquotedblright{}). Between them they cover most of what English does with \emph{in} and \emph{on}.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Ich wohne in …}
Put a place after it and the sentence is finished:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich wohne in Berlin.} — \textquotedblleft{}I live in Berlin.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Swap the city for your own and the sentence is yours. This is the first thing in this book you can say about your actual life without being handed the whole line.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} — short \emph{i}, exactly as in English
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich wohne in Berlin.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the same sentence with the town you actually live in
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{in} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}In\textquotedblright{} — unchanged.) Say where you live. (\emph{Ich wohne in …}) Which word covers \textquotedblleft{}on\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Auf}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[wo]{wo — \textquotedblleft{}where,\textquotedblright{} and the German w-questions}

\label{lesson:GE-C05-wo}



\begin{quote}
You can say where you live. To \emph{ask} it, you need the question word — and it belongs to a family you have already started.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: wo}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{wo} — \textquotedblleft{}where.\textquotedblright{} Said \emph{voh}, a long \emph{oh}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Wo wohnst du?} — \textquotedblleft{}Where do you live?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Note there is no extra \textquotedblleft{}do\textquotedblright{} in German. English needs \emph{do} to ask a question; German simply puts the question word first and the verb straight after it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{wo} is English \textbf{where} with the \emph{-re} worn away. And it is not alone — German's question words are the English ones with \textbf{wh-} flattened to \textbf{w-}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{wo} & where \\
\emph{wie} & how \\
\emph{wer} & who \\
\emph{wann} & when \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English spells them \emph{wh-} and mostly says them \emph{w-}; German just spells what it says. Once you spot the family, each new one costs almost nothing.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}wo\textquotedblright{} (\emph{voh}) — where
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Wo wohnst du?\textquotedblright{} — no \textquotedblleft{}do\textquotedblright{} needed
  \item the family — \textquotedblleft{}wo\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}wie\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}wer\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}wann\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{wo} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Where.\textquotedblright{}) Ask someone where they live. (\emph{Wo wohnst du?}) What happened to English \emph{wh-} in German? (It flattened to \emph{w-}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[machen]{machen — \textquotedblleft{}to make,\textquotedblright{} and it is exactly English \emph{make}}

\label{lesson:GE-C05-machen}



\begin{quote}
Second verb — and it needs no new grammar at all. The stem-plus-ending machine you built on \emph{wohnen} runs it unchanged.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: machen}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{machen} — \textquotedblleft{}to make,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}to do.\textquotedblright{} German uses one verb for both.
\end{quote}

Stem: \textbf{mach-}. So \emph{ich mache}, \emph{du machst}, \emph{er macht}, \emph{wir machen}, \emph{ihr macht}, \emph{sie machen}. Nothing new — that is the payoff of a regular pattern.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{ch-ach} — the \textbf{ch} after \emph{a} is the raspy throat sound you met in \emph{Nacht}, the \emph{ch} of Scottish \emph{loch}. Not the soft \emph{ich} sound.
\end{itemize}

So: \emph{MAKH-en}, with a clean open \emph{ah}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{machen} is English \textbf{make}, from Germanic \emph{makōn}, \textquotedblleft{}to shape, to fit together.\textquotedblright{} The \emph{k} became the \emph{ch} rasp on the way, by the same High German consonant shift that gave you \emph{gut} from \emph{good}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{German} \\
\midrule
ma\textbf{k}e & ma\textbf{ch}en \\
i\textbf{k} (old \emph{I}) & i\textbf{ch} \\
boo\textbf{k} & Bu\textbf{ch} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{machen} is \emph{make}, wearing German pronunciation.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}machen\textquotedblright{} (\emph{MAKH-en}) — the \emph{loch} rasp
  \item \textquotedblleft{}make\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}machen\textquotedblright{}; \textquotedblleft{}book\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Buch\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich mache\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}du machst\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}er macht\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{machen} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To make,\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}to do.\textquotedblright{}) Which English word is it? (\emph{Make}.) Which \emph{ch} does it use? (The raspy \emph{ach}, not the soft \emph{ich}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[was]{was — \textquotedblleft{}what,\textquotedblright{} and the t-to-s swap one last time}

\label{lesson:GE-C05-was}



\begin{quote}
You have \emph{wo}. Here is its most useful sibling, and you can already predict how it is spelt.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: was}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{was} — \textquotedblleft{}what.\textquotedblright{} Said \emph{vass}, short \emph{a}, crisp \emph{s}.
\end{quote}

You met the rule that makes it: where English keeps a final \textbf{t}, German shows an \textbf{s}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{German} \\
\midrule
wha\textbf{t} & wa\textbf{s} \\
tha\textbf{t} & da\textbf{s} \\
i\textbf{t} & e\textbf{s} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Third time you have seen this pair, and the last new word it gives you.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Was machst du?}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Was machst du?} — \textquotedblleft{}What are you doing?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Question word first, verb second, subject third — the same shape as \emph{Wo wohnst du?}. And note again that German needs no \textquotedblleft{}do\textquotedblright{}: \emph{machst} carries the whole question.

There is also no separate \textquotedblleft{}am …-ing\textquotedblright{} form in German. \emph{Was machst du?} covers both \textquotedblleft{}what do you do?\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}what are you doing?\textquotedblright{} — context decides.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}was\textquotedblright{} (\emph{vass}) — what
  \item \textquotedblleft{}what/was\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}that/das\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}it/es\textquotedblright{} — the swap three times
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Was machst du?\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Wo wohnst du?\textquotedblright{} — the same shape
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{was} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}What.\textquotedblright{}) Which swap explains its spelling? (English \emph{t} shows up as German \emph{s}.) Ask what someone is doing. (\emph{Was machst du?})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lernen]{lernen — \textquotedblleft{}to learn,\textquotedblright{} and its noun is \emph{lore}}

\label{lesson:GE-C05-lernen}



\begin{quote}
Third verb, same machine — and this is the one you are going to need to describe what you are doing right now.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: lernen}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{lernen} — \textquotedblleft{}to learn.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Stem \textbf{lern-}: \emph{ich lerne}, \emph{du lernst}, \emph{er lernt}. Three verbs now, one pattern.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{r-uvular-german} — the German \textbf{r} is a soft scrape at the back of the throat, nothing like the English \emph{r} made with the tongue tip.
\end{itemize}

So: \emph{LER-nen}, with a short \emph{e} as in English \emph{bed}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{lernen} is English \textbf{learn} — the same Germanic root, barely disguised.

Its relatives are the good part. The German noun is \textbf{die Lehre}, \textquotedblleft{}the teaching, the body of what is taught\textquotedblright{} — and that word is English \textbf{lore}. Folklore is the \emph{Lehre} of a folk; the lore of a craft is what its learners have accumulated.

So German kept the verb and the noun in the same family, and English kept both too — it just stopped noticing that \emph{learn} and \emph{lore} were relatives.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}lernen\textquotedblright{} (\emph{LER-nen}) — scrape the \emph{r} at the back
  \item \textquotedblleft{}lernen\textquotedblright{} and English \textquotedblleft{}learn\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}die Lehre\textquotedblright{} and English \textquotedblleft{}lore\textquotedblright{} — folklore
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{lernen} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To learn.\textquotedblright{}) What is its noun, and which English word is that? (\emph{Die Lehre}; \emph{lore}.) Give the \emph{ich} form. (\emph{Ich lerne}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Deutsch]{Deutsch — the language, and it means \textquotedblleft{}of the people\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C05-deutsch}



\begin{quote}
One noun stands between you and a sentence about what you are doing right now — the name of the language itself.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Deutsch}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Deutsch} — \textquotedblleft{}German,\textquotedblright{} the language.
\end{quote}

Capital \textbf{D}, because a language name is a noun and German capitalises every noun.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{eu-diphthong} — German \textbf{eu} is the \emph{oy} of English \emph{boy}.
  \item \texttt{tsch-ch} — \textbf{tsch} is the \emph{tch} of English \emph{match}, the same cluster that opens \emph{tschüss}.
\end{itemize}

So: \emph{DOYTCH}, one syllable.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Deutsch} comes from Old High German \textbf{diutisc}, \textquotedblleft{}of the people, of the folk.\textquotedblright{} The Germanic tribes simply called their own tongue \emph{the people's language} — as opposed to Latin, the language of church and administration.

That root travelled a long way:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Word} & \textbf{Language} & \textbf{Route} \\
\midrule
\emph{Deutsch} & German & \emph{diutisc}, \textquotedblleft{}of the people\textquotedblright{} \\
\textbf{Dutch} & English & the same word, later narrowed to the Netherlands \\
\textbf{Teutonic} & English & via Latin \emph{Teutonicus} \\
\emph{Tedesco} & Italian & its own echo of \emph{diutisc} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So English \textbf{Dutch} and German \textbf{Deutsch} are not lookalikes — they are one word that drifted apart, and English simply pointed it at a smaller country.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Deutsch\textquotedblright{} (\emph{DOYTCH}) — one syllable
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Deutsch\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Dutch\textquotedblright{} — the same old word
  \item what it meant — \textquotedblleft{}of the people\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{Deutsch} literally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Of the people.\textquotedblright{}) Which English word is the same word? (\emph{Dutch}.) Why the capital \textbf{D}? (It is a noun.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Ich lerne Deutsch]{Ich lerne Deutsch — your first real sentence}

\label{lesson:GE-C05-ich-lerne-deutsch}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new is coming. Every piece of the next line has had its own lesson — and that is exactly the point.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Ich lerne Deutsch}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich lerne Deutsch.} — \textquotedblleft{}I am learning German.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Piece} & \textbf{Where it came from} \\
\midrule
\emph{ich} & the introductions chapter \\
\emph{lern-} & the stem of \emph{lernen} \\
\emph{-e} & the \emph{ich} ending \\
\emph{Deutsch} & the last lesson \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

This is the first sentence in the book that was \textbf{not handed to you}. You built it: a pronoun, a stem, an ending, a noun. Change any piece and it still works.

Remember there is no separate \textquotedblleft{}am …-ing\textquotedblright{} in German. \emph{Ich lerne} covers both \textquotedblleft{}I learn\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}I am learning,\textquotedblright{} so this one line does the work of two English tenses.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: swap the pieces}]
The same slots take other words, and you already have all of them:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Ich wohne in Berlin.} · \emph{Was machst du?} · \emph{Ich lerne Deutsch.}
\end{quote}

Three sentences, one machine. From here the language is combinations, not memorised lines.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich lerne Deutsch.\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ikh LER-neh DOYTCH}
  \item it in pieces — \textquotedblleft{}ich\textquotedblright{}, "lern-", \textquotedblleft{}-e\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}Deutsch\textquotedblright{}
  \item all three sentences in a row
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I am learning German.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Ich lerne Deutsch.}) Which four pieces is it made of? (\emph{Ich}, the stem \emph{lern-}, the ending \emph{-e}, and \emph{Deutsch}.) How does German say \textquotedblleft{}I am learning\textquotedblright{} as opposed to \textquotedblleft{}I learn\textquotedblright{}? (It does not — \emph{ich lerne} is both.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(the overt subject)]{Why German keeps the pronoun}

\label{lesson:GE-C05-pronomen-regel}



\begin{quote}
Here is the puzzle left open earlier. German endings \emph{do} say who the subject is. So why say \emph{ich} at all?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three languages, three reasons}]
Spanish, French and German each decide differently, and for different reasons:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{The pronoun} & \textbf{Why} \\
\midrule
Spanish & \textbf{dropped} & \emph{hablo} already says \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} \\
French & \textbf{kept} & its endings are silent, so the pronoun is the only clue \\
German & \textbf{kept} & its grammar demands an overt subject \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The German reason is the interesting one, because it is \emph{not} about sound. German endings are perfectly audible — you proved that a few lessons ago. The pronoun stays because a German sentence is built around the \textbf{verb in second position}, with something standing in front of it. Drop \emph{ich} and there is nothing to hold that first slot.

So German keeps the pronoun for \textbf{structure}, French for \textbf{sound}, and Spanish keeps neither because it needs neither. Three answers, and only one of them is about being understood.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich lerne Deutsch.\textquotedblright{} — with the pronoun, always
  \item the three reasons — Spanish drops, French keeps for sound, German keeps for structure
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich wohne\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}ich mache\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}ich lerne\textquotedblright{} — never without the \emph{ich}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does German keep the pronoun? (Its grammar needs an overt subject — the verb sits second, so something must come first.) Why does French? (Its endings are silent.) Why does Spanish not need to? (\emph{Hablo} already says \textquotedblleft{}I.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — building sentences, not reciting them}

\label{lesson:GE-C05-practice}



\begin{quote}
For the first time you are \emph{building} German rather than repeating it. Run each verb through the three singular persons.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three verbs, one pattern}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Verb} & \textbf{\emph{ich} · \emph{du} · \emph{er}} \\
\midrule
\emph{wohnen} & \emph{wohne} · \emph{wohnst} · \emph{wohnt} \\
\emph{machen} & \emph{mache} · \emph{machst} · \emph{macht} \\
\emph{lernen} & \emph{lerne} · \emph{lernst} · \emph{lernt} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The same endings every time — \textbf{-e}, \textbf{-st}, \textbf{-t} — and, unlike French, you can hear all three. You still keep the pronoun, because German needs an overt subject.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{Wo wohnst du?} & Where do you live? \\
\emph{Ich wohne in Berlin. Und du?} & I live in Berlin. And you? \\
\emph{Ich wohne in Wien. Was machst du?} & I live in Vienna. What are you doing? \\
\emph{Ich lerne Deutsch!} & I'm learning German! \\
\emph{Sehr gut!} & Very good! \\
\emph{Danke!} — \emph{Bitte.} & Thanks! — You're welcome. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every line is assembled from pieces you own. Nothing here was memorised whole.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the whole exchange, both voices
  \item each verb through \emph{ich} / \emph{du} / \emph{er}
  \item the exchange again with your own city
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Wo wohnst du? — Ich wohne in …\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the three singular endings, and can you hear them? (\emph{-e}, \emph{-st}, \emph{-t}; yes — unlike French.) Give the \emph{ich} form of all three verbs. (\emph{Ich wohne}, \emph{ich mache}, \emph{ich lerne}.) Why keep the pronoun? (German needs an overt subject.)
\end{tcolorbox}
